objectives: Find the first position whose value is at least a target (the lower bound).
Count values with a lower bound, including duplicates and missing values.
Count cells in a grid sorted by rows and columns with a staircase walk.

sections.heading: Intuition: find where a value starts
paragraphs: Exact search answers "is it here?" Many questions are about where a group starts instead. In the sorted list [1, 3, 3, 3, 8], the 3s start at index 1. That index is also how many values are smaller than 3.
The first index whose value is at least x is called the lower bound of x. It exists even when x isn't in the list: for 4 it's index 4, where the 8 is, meaning four values are smaller than 4.

callout.text: The lower bound is a first-true search from day 9 with the question "is values[i] ≥ x?". Every no comes before every yes because the list is sorted.

diagram.description: Sorted values 1, 3, 3, 3, 8. Index 1, the first 3, is the lower bound of 3.

sections.heading: Baseline: scan until the value is big enough
paragraphs: Walking from the left until you reach a value ≥ x finds the lower bound in O(n). With many duplicates or many questions, binary search's O(log n) per question is much faster.

sections.heading: Worked example: count the scores below a cutoff
paragraphs: Use the hi-excluded range from day 8, starting with lo = 0 and hi = n. hi = n means "maybe every value is below x".
If values[mid] < x, the first value ≥ x is after mid: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid could be the first one: hi = mid. When lo = hi, that's the lower bound, and it's also the count of values below x.
The three cases in the player cover a value with duplicates (3), a missing value (4), and a value bigger than everything (10), where the answer is n.

sections.heading: Worked example: count small values in a sorted grid
paragraphs: In a grid where every row increases left to right and every column increases top to bottom, you can count the cells ≤ x without looking at all of them.

Start at the bottom-left corner. It's the largest value in its column and the smallest in its row. If it's ≤ x, the whole column above it is ≤ x too: count those cells and move right. If it's > x, the rest of its row is even larger: move up. Each step rules out a whole row or column, so it takes at most rows + columns steps.

sections.heading: Your turn: Count Negative Numbers in a Sorted Matrix
paragraphs: A grid is sorted in non-increasing order along each row and each column. Count its negative numbers.

sections.heading: Your turn: Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target
paragraphs: Given a sorted list of letters and a target letter, return the smallest letter in the list that is strictly greater than the target. If there isn't one, wrap around and return the first letter.

callout.text: "At least" and "strictly greater" are different questions. Which one do you need, and what does it change in the lower bound loop?

sections.heading: Your turn: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
paragraphs: Today's medium. Given a sorted array that may contain duplicates, return the first and last index of a target, or [-1, -1] if it isn't there. It must run in O(log n).

callout.text: The lower bound gives you one end. Work out the yes/no question whose first yes would give you the other end, and test it on [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10] with target 8.
callout.title: Where to start

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: A lower bound takes O(log n). The staircase count takes O(rows + columns), which beats checking all rows × columns cells.
Be clear about which question you're asking: "≥ x" and "> x" give different indexes whenever x appears in the list.

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: What is the lower bound of 4 in [1, 3, 3, 3, 8], and why is it useful?
checks.answer: Index 4. It's the count of values below 4, and it's where 4 would be inserted.

checks.prompt: In the staircase walk, why is it safe to count a whole column at once?
checks.answer: The current cell is ≤ x and it's the largest in its column so far, so every cell above it is ≤ x too.

checks.prompt: Why can't the staircase start at the top-left corner?
checks.answer: The top-left is the smallest in both its row and column, so neither outcome rules out a whole row or column.
